question: What is the primary reason researchers use sampling instead of studying an entire population?

options.A: It completely eliminates all types of research bias.
options.B: It is often impractical, costly, and time-consuming to study everyone.
options.C: It is only required for qualitative nursing research studies.
options.D: It guarantees 100% generalizability to every global healthcare setting.

explanation: Studying an entire population is usually impractical, costly, and time-consuming, which is why researchers select a representative subset instead. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h1)

question: Why is understanding sampling methodology crucial for nursing students?

options.A: To ensure evidence-based practice is built on trustworthy and valid research findings.
options.B: To avoid ever having to write a research proposal.
options.C: To replace the need for ethical committee approval.
options.D: To guarantee that all patients receive the exact same treatment.

explanation: A solid grasp of sampling strategies helps students critically appraise literature and ensure research findings used in practice are valid. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h1)

question: How is the target population best defined in nursing research?

options.A: The exact group of patients who agree to participate in the study.
options.B: The entire group of individuals the researcher is interested in and wants to generalize results to.
options.C: The small group of nurses who assist with data collection.
options.D: The patients who are physically present in a single hospital ward on a given day.

explanation: The target population represents the full aggregation of cases the researcher wishes to study and make generalizations about. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h2)

question: What distinguishes the accessible population from the target population?

options.A: The accessible population is the specific subset of the target population that is actually available and feasible to study.
options.B: The accessible population includes every single member of the global healthcare community.
options.C: The accessible population is only used in qualitative pilot studies.
options.D: There is no difference; the terms are completely interchangeable.

explanation: The accessible population is the portion of the target population that researchers can realistically reach and recruit for their study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of inclusion criteria in a nursing research study?

options.A: To eliminate all potential participants from the study.
options.B: To define the key characteristics prospective participants must possess to be eligible.
options.C: To identify individuals who should be banned from receiving nursing care.
options.D: To increase the cost and duration of the research project.

explanation: Inclusion criteria outline the specific traits required for individuals to qualify for participation in the research study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h3)

question: Why are exclusion criteria important in clinical nursing research?

options.A: They help control confounding variables and protect vulnerable populations from harm.
options.B: They ensure that every nurse in the hospital becomes a participant.
options.C: They replace the need for informed consent.
options.D: They make the sample size as large as the entire target population.

explanation: Exclusion criteria filter out characteristics that could confound results or pose safety risks, safeguarding both data integrity and patient safety. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h3)

question: What is a defining characteristic of probability sampling techniques?

options.A: Participants are chosen based on their convenience and availability.
options.B: Every member of the accessible population has a known, non-zero probability of being selected.
options.C: The researcher handpicks participants who best represent personal opinions.
options.D: It is exclusively used in qualitative nursing research.

explanation: Probability sampling uses random selection so that every population member has a known chance of being included in the study. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h4)

question: In which sampling technique is the population divided into subgroups, with random samples then drawn from each subgroup?
explanation: Stratified random sampling divides the population into homogeneous strata and draws random samples from each to ensure representation. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h4)

question: Why do nurse researchers sometimes choose non-probability sampling despite its limitations?

options.A: It completely eliminates sampling error and bias.
options.B: It is often more practical, economical, and useful when studying hard-to-reach populations.
options.C: It is legally mandated by international nursing boards.
options.D: It guarantees 100% generalizability to all global populations.

explanation: Non-probability sampling is often used due to practical constraints and when studying populations where random frames are unavailable. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h5)

question: Which non-probability sampling method relies on current participants to refer future study participants?
explanation: Snowball sampling uses referrals from initial participants to build the sample, which is especially useful for hard-to-reach populations. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h5)

question: What is the consequence of having a sample size that is too small in a quantitative nursing study?

options.A: It guarantees a Type I error.
options.B: It may lead to a Type II error, missing a true clinical effect due to low statistical power.
options.C: It increases the cost of the study unnecessarily.
options.D: It makes generalizability to the target population completely foolproof.

explanation: An inadequate sample size reduces statistical power, increasing the risk of failing to detect a real effect (Type II error). [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h6)

question: What does statistical power represent in research design?

options.A: The financial budget allocated for patient recruitment.
options.B: The probability that a study will correctly reject a false null hypothesis.
options.C: The total number of hospitals participating in the research.
options.D: The percentage of dropouts during data collection.

explanation: Statistical power is the likelihood that a research study will successfully detect an effect when it actually exists. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h6)

question: What is the key difference between sampling error and sampling bias?

options.A: Sampling error is random natural variation, whereas sampling bias is systematic error due to flawed selection procedures.
options.B: Sampling error only occurs in qualitative studies, while bias only occurs in quantitative studies.
options.C: Sampling bias can be eliminated by increasing sample size, but sampling error cannot.
options.D: There is no difference; both terms mean exactly the same thing.

explanation: Sampling error is expected random variance, whereas sampling bias represents systematic flaws that make a sample unrepresentative. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h7)

question: How can researchers best minimize random sampling error in a quantitative study?

options.B: By increasing the sample size and utilizing proper probability sampling techniques.
options.C: By ignoring outliers in the data set.
options.D: By narrowing inclusion criteria until only one patient remains.

explanation: Increasing sample size and employing robust probability sampling methods help reduce random sampling error. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T17#GNS224_U1_T17_h7)
